problem:
Consider the following differential equation

$$
{y}^{″}+4y=2\operatorname{tan}⁡x.
$$

The general solution to this equation can be written as

$$
y(x)=A\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+B\operatorname{sin}⁡2x+g(x),
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are constants. Which of the following could be the function $g(x)?$

*Hint: Use the variation of parameters method. You may also wish to make use of the following results (integration constants omitted):*

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{sin}⁡2x\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =x-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x \\ \int \operatorname{cos}⁡2x\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{cos}⁡x|-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x-\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

activity_context.topic_title: Solving Second-Order ODEs Using Variation of Parameters

feedback.problem:
Consider the following differential equation

$$
{y}^{″}+4y={csc}^{3}⁡2x.
$$

The general solution to this equation can be written as

$$
y(x)=P\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡2x+g(x),
$$

where $P$ and $Q$ are constants. Which of the following could be the function $g(x)?$

*Hint: Use the variation of parameters method. You may also wish to make use of the following result:*

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡4x=2{cos}^{2}⁡2x-1\end{aligned}
$$
feedback.worked_solution:
Suppose we have a second-order linear differential equation with linearly independent fundamental solutions ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x).$ Then, according to the method of variation of parameters, we can seek a particular solution ${y}_{p}$ using the ansatz

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}(x) & ={u}_{1}(x){y}_{1}(x)+{u}_{2}(x){y}_{2}(x),\end{aligned}
$$

where ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}$ satisfy the following system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}^{′}{y}_{1}^{′}+{u}_{2}^{′}{y}_{2}^{′}=f(x) \\ {u}_{1}^{′}{y}_{1}+{u}_{2}^{′}{y}_{2}=0\end{aligned}
$$

The solution to this system is

$$
{u}_{1}(x)=-\int \frac{f(x){y}_{2}(x)}{W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})}\,dx,\,{u}_{2}(x)=\int \frac{f(x){y}_{1}(x)}{W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})}\,dx,
$$

where $W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})$ is the Wronskian.

First, we note that the forcing term is $f(x)={csc}^{3}⁡2x.$

From the given information, we see that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}(x)=P\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡2x.
$$

Therefore, the fundamental solutions to the corresponding homogeneous equation are

$$
{y}_{1}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡2x,\,{y}_{2}(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡2x.
$$

We can use the method of variation of parameters if these solutions are independent. So, let's first compute the Wronskian:

$$
\begin{aligned}W({y}_{1},{y}_{2}) & =|\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}^{′} & {y}_{2}^{′}\end{aligned}| \\  & ={y}_{1}(x){y}_{2}^{′}(x)-{y}_{1}^{′}(x){y}_{2}(x) \\  & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡2x)(\operatorname{sin}⁡2x)^{′}-(\operatorname{cos}⁡2x)^{′}(\operatorname{sin}⁡2x) \\  & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡2x)(2\operatorname{cos}⁡2x)-(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2x)(\operatorname{sin}⁡2x) \\  & =2{cos}^{2}⁡2x+2{sin}^{2}⁡2x \\  & =2\ne 0\end{aligned}
$$

Since the Wronskian is not equal to zero, this confirms that the functions  ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x)$ are independent. 

Let's compute ${u}_{1}(x)$ and ${u}_{2}(x)$:

- First, we compute ${u}_{1}(x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}(x) & =-\int \frac{{csc}^{3}⁡2x\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡2x}{2}\,dx \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\int {csc}^{2}⁡2x\,dx \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{cot}⁡2x\end{aligned}
$$

- Then, we compute ${u}_{2}(x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{2}(x) & =\int \frac{{csc}^{3}⁡2x\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡2x}{2}\,dx \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡2x}{{sin}^{3}⁡2x}\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

Let $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡2x.$ Then $du=2\operatorname{cos}⁡2x\,dx,$ so $\operatorname{cos}⁡2x\,dx=\frac{1}{2}\,du,$ and the integral becomes

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡2x}{{sin}^{3}⁡2x}\,dx & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{{u}^{3}}(\frac{1}{2}\,du) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\int {u}^{-3}\,du \\  & =-\frac{1}{8}{u}^{-2} \\  & =-\frac{1}{8{sin}^{2}⁡2x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}(x) & ={u}_{1}{y}_{1}+{u}_{2}{y}_{2} \\  & =(\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{cot}⁡2x)(\operatorname{cos}⁡2x)+(-\frac{1}{8{sin}^{2}⁡2x})(\operatorname{sin}⁡2x) \\  & =\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡2x}{4\operatorname{sin}⁡2x}-\frac{1}{8\operatorname{sin}⁡2x} \\  & =\frac{1}{8\operatorname{sin}⁡2x}(2{cos}^{2}⁡2x-1) \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡4x}{8\operatorname{sin}⁡2x} \\  & =\frac{1}{8}\operatorname{cos}⁡4x\,\operatorname{csc}⁡2x.\end{aligned}
$$

The general solution is the sum of the complementary and particular solutions, and can be written as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & ={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x) \\  & =P\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡2x\,+\,{{\frac{1}{8}\operatorname{cos}⁡4x\operatorname{csc}⁡2x}_{⏟}}_{g(x)}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
g(x)=\frac{1}{8}\operatorname{cos}⁡4x\operatorname{csc}⁡2x.
$$
